title: Tu B'Av
hookLine: the fifteenth of Av, once a day when young women danced in white in the vineyards (Mishnah Taanit 4:8)

cards: Rows of vines outside Jerusalem. Young women walk out between them, all dressed in white, and begin to dance.
It sounds like the opening of a romance, but it's in the Mishnah, a collection of Jewish law and teaching, at the close of a section about fast days.
In the middle of all that seriousness, a rabbi stops to remember a day of pure joy. Its name is a date on the Hebrew calendar: the fifteenth of the month of Av.

teach.h: NO DAYS OF JOY LIKE THESE.
teach.b: First, the saying. In the Mishnah, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says, in plain words, that Israel had no days of joy like the fifteenth of Av and the Day of Atonement.
On those days, the daughters of Jerusalem went out in white garments and danced in the vineyards. Second, the detail that makes the passage.

The white garments were borrowed, the Mishnah says, so as not to shame anyone who had none of her own. Rich or poor, nobody could tell. On a day about love, the first act was a kindness about dignity.
The young women called out to the young men, in plain words: lift up your eyes and see whom you choose; don't look at beauty, look at family.
The Mishnah then reads a line from the Song of Songs about a king on the day of his wedding, and the gladness of his heart. Fourth, the name.
Tu is the number fifteen written in Hebrew letters, and Av is the month, so the name is simply the date. The vineyard dances belong to the past.
Some Jews mark the day today as a day for love, for weddings and for matchmaking, a happy turn in a month that also holds the mourning of Tisha B'Av.
This week traced love's edges: boundaries, loving yourself, small acts, listening, grief, and a note. Tu B'Av adds one more: when love dances, nobody gets left out of the white.

how: Some Jews today mark Tu B'Av as a day of love, with weddings, matchmaking events and celebrations, and Jews who study the Mishnah read about it in tractate Taanit.

games.q: it's the fifteenth of Av in Jerusalem, and you own a beautiful white dress. what does the Mishnah say the young women did?
o: wear your own, the finest you have.
stay home if you have nothing white.
games.why: the white garments were borrowed, so as not to shame anyone who had none of her own. on a day of love, nobody could tell rich from poor.

practice: Bring to mind a time someone made sure you weren't left out, an invitation, a seat saved, a coat lent, a word that put you on equal footing, and stay with it for a breath or two.
Then let one person around you who might be on the outside right now come to mind, someone new, someone quiet, someone without the right thing to wear in whatever sense, and simply hold them kindly.
If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words.
